questions.q: What is the key structural difference between a security audit and a bug bounty program?
options: They are functionally identical and interchangeable in every respect
A bug bounty always happens before launch, and an audit always happens after
An audit is a fixed-duration engagement that ends with a report, while a bug bounty is an open-ended program that runs indefinitely after launch
An audit never produces a report, only a bug bounty does
questions.explain: An audit is time-boxed and concludes with a report; a bug bounty has no fixed end date and keeps running as long as the protocol is live.

questions.q: Why does relying on only an audit, without an ongoing bug bounty, leave a coverage gap?
options: Audits can only review already-deployed contracts, never pre-launch code
Audits are more expensive than bug bounties and therefore worse value
There is no gap -- an audit alone provides complete, permanent coverage
The audit doesn't keep watching the code after its fixed engagement ends, leaving no coverage for the period after launch
questions.explain: An audit is a snapshot review for a defined window; it provides no ongoing protection once that engagement concludes and the protocol keeps evolving or facing new attack attempts.

questions.q: Why does a bug bounty's maximum payout size function as a market signal?
options: Payout size has no effect on how much attention a bounty program receives
Higher payouts always guarantee zero vulnerabilities will ever be found
A protocol is competing for serious researcher attention against every other active bounty on the market, and a low payout relative to comparable programs attracts less scrutiny
All bug bounty programs are required by law to offer identical payouts
questions.explain: Researchers choose where to spend their time; a bounty priced low relative to comparable programs gets less serious attention, similar to an underpriced job listing.

questions.q: Why are severity-tiered bounty payouts calculated as a percentage of funds at risk, rather than a flat amount?
options: Flat amounts are always preferred over percentage-based payouts in practice
To ensure every finding, regardless of severity, pays the exact same amount
To make responsibly disclosing a vulnerability more profitable than exploiting it, for a rational researcher weighing both options
Percentage-based payouts have no relationship to deterring exploitation
questions.explain: Scaling payout to the actual funds at risk is deliberate economic design -- it's meant to beat the payoff of exploiting the same vulnerability.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what does Lesson 28 cover as the next layer of protection, on top of audits and bounties?
options: Returning to Chapter 3 to reverify the contract's source code
Rewriting the contract's test suite from Chapter 1 entirely
Choosing a new RPC provider for production use
Phased rollouts and value caps, limiting how much a contract can actually lose even after being audited and bountied
questions.explain: Lesson 28 adds another layer of risk reduction -- value caps and phased rollouts -- recognizing that audits and bounties reduce but don't eliminate risk.
